Introduction Firm performance prediction models are widely used to assess the financial health and future outcomes of companies, offering valuable support for data-driven decision-making (Borchert et al., 2023). These models are instrumental for loan officers evaluating corporate creditworthiness, insurance brokers setting premiums, investment analysts assessing potential risks and returns, credit agencies advising on business reliability, and banking regulators monitoring systemic financial stability. Consequently, accurate and robust financial performance prediction models carry significant economic relevance and serve as essential tools for informed financial and strategic decision-making (Arno et al., 2025). While many earlier studies on financial performance and corporate failure (Lukason & Laitinen, 2019; Önder & Altintaş, 2017) have relied heavily on financial ratios, this approach has notable limitations. Adnan Aziz & Dar (2006) contend that such ratios can be effective in forecasting performance. However, several critiques highlight their potential unreliability—particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises that may not consistently publish financial statements. Moreover, financial reports can be manipulated to serve strategic interests (Mousa et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2014), leading to distorted ratio values and potentially flawed predictions. Understanding the key determinants of financial performance remains a core focus in both corporate finance and strategic management. Managerial capability and efficiency are essential metrics for evaluating the performance of business operations (Amirteimoori & Allahviranloo, 2025). In particular, operational efficiency has gained increasing attention due to its ability to drive profitability, enhance competitiveness, and support long-term sustainability. Despite its theoretical relevance, the integration of efficiency metrics—especially those derived from non-parametric frontier techniques like Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA)—into predictive models is still relatively underexplored, particularly in emerging market contexts. Traditional models often rely on linear regression techniques and financial ratios, which may fail to capture the complex, nonlinear relationships between firm attributes and performance outcomes. To overcome these limitations, the present study explores the role of firm efficiency in predicting financial performance, proposing an alternative approach that goes beyond conventional financial ratios. By incorporating DEA-based efficiency scores into a machine learning (ML) framework, the research aims to deliver more reliable and accurate performance predictions. The focus is on non-financial firms listed on the Egyptian Stock Exchange from 2016 to 2022—a context where operational and financial constraints often differ significantly from those in developed markets. The study is guided by two primary objectives: (1) to assess whether the inclusion of DEA-based efficiency measures enhances the predictive accuracy of performance models, and (2) to identify the key variables that drive financial performance while developing a robust prediction model using interpretable advanced ML techniques. These objectives are particularly important in the Egyptian context, where the adoption of advanced data-driven methodologies remains in its early stages. This research offers significant and original contributions to the literature by introducing a novel hybrid approach to predicting financial performance, combining DEA-based efficiency measures with advanced ML. While prior research has examined the firm efficiency on financial performance (Baik et al., 2013; Dahunsi & Soetan, 2022; Peng et al., 2025; Thien et al., 2024), most studies have relied on traditional statistical techniques that present several limitations. These conventional methods typically emphasize the direction of relationships—positive or negative—when identifying significant predictors, often overlooking the form of the relationship, whether linear or nonlinear. Such oversights may lead to biased or incomplete findings. To address the limitations of traditional statistical methods and individual ML models, I develop a Super Learner ensemble that integrates a tuned Random Forest (RF) and Categorical Gradient Boosting (CatBoost) with a linear regression meta- learner. The Super Learner, introduced by van der Laan et al., is a stacking-based ensemble learning algorithm designed to enhance predictive performance by optimally combining multiple base models through a meta-learning framework. Unlike single-model approaches, the Super Learner adaptively weights and integrates predictions from diverse algorithms, thereby improving both accuracy and robustness. Its dynamic selection of the most effective base models for a given task enables it to consistently outperform individual models across various datasets. Furthermore, by minimizing the influence of poorly performing models, the Super Learner reduces overfitting and enhances generalization to new data. The meta-learner plays a pivotal role in this process, learning the optimal combination of base model predictions to minimize overall error. As a result, the Super Learner ensemble offers a powerful and reliable predictive framework, well-suited for capturing complex relationships and delivering accurate forecasts of financial performance. This study makes several important contributions to the existing literature. First, it provides empirical support for incorporating DEA-based efficiency scores into financial performance prediction models, particularly in the context of a developing economy. Second, it introduces a novel Super Learner ensemble regression model, specifically designed to address the complexities of financial performance prediction, demonstrating significant improvements over traditional approaches. Third, the model’s performance is rigorously evaluated using a range of statistical metrics and compared against baseline statistical models, individual ML algorithms, and other ensemble methods, including bagging, boosting, voting, and stacked ensembles. The findings consistently highlight the superior predictive accuracy and robustness of the proposed model. Fourth, by employing CatBoost for feature importance analysis, the study identifies the most influential variables driving financial performance, offering valuable insights for investors and other stakeholders aiming to make well-informed decisions. Finally, to enhance interpretability, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) are used to explain the global structure of the model and the effect of each variable, ensuring transparency without compromising performance. Collectively, these contributions advance the literature on firm efficiency and performance prediction, while offering practical guidance for investors, policymakers, and corporate managers operating in complex and dynamic market environments. Empirical results confirm that the Super Learner model that incorporated DEA substantially outperforms both traditional linear regression and standalone ML approaches in predicting financial performance. The model achieves the highest performance across multiple metrics, including an R-squared (R²) of 0.612, root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.061, and mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.046. The results provide strong empirical support for the inclusion of firm efficiency in predictive models. A t-test confirms that the 3.8% increase in R² from including DEA is statistically significant at the 1% level. SHAP and partial dependence analyses show that while DEA efficiency, net working capital, and cash holdings maintain positive nonlinear relationships with performance, leverage follows a distinct concave pattern. Theoretical Underpinnings Firm efficiency has long been recognized as a critical driver of financial performance, rooted in several foundational theories in economics and management. The efficient-structure hypothesis, as discussed by Dudu & Kilicaslan (2009), posits that firms with superior operational, technological, or managerial efficiency can achieve higher profitability and dominate market share, leading to naturally concentrated markets without necessarily reducing consumer welfare. In contrast, the market-power hypothesis contends that profitability often stems from anti-competitive practices rather than genuine efficiency gains. Their empirical study of Turkish manufacturing firms using stochastic frontier analysis revealed that the relevance of these competing hypotheses varies across industries, suggesting that financial performance is context-dependent and shaped by both efficiency and market dynamics. Several economic and management theories explain how operational efficiency influences firm profitability. These theories emphasize cost reduction, competitive advantage, and resource optimization as key drivers of financial performance. Below are the primary theoretical perspectives: 2.1 Resource-Based View (RBV) The Resource-Based View (RBV) posits that firms achieve sustained profitability by leveraging unique, valuable, and difficult-to-imitate resources (Barney, 1991). Efficiency improvements—such as better utilization of physical assets (PP&E), cost management (COGS, SG&A), and workforce productivity—enhance a firm’s competitive advantage. Efficient firms generate higher returns by minimizing waste and maximizing output from limited inputs. Empirical studies confirm that firms with superior efficiency metrics (e.g., DEA scores) exhibit stronger profitability (Demerjian et al., 2012). 2.2 Dynamic Capabilities Theory Teece et al. (1997) argue that firms with dynamic capabilities—abilities to adapt processes and resources—sustain profitability by continuously improving efficiency. For example, efficient firms optimize supply chains (e.g., just-in-time inventory) or adopt advanced production technologies, reducing costs and boosting margins. The Malmquist index in DEA captures such improvements by separating technical efficiency change (better resource use) from technology change (innovation) (Färe et al., 1992). 2.3 Agency Theory Jensen & Meckling (1976) emphasize that agency costs—such as managerial slack—can diminish profitability. They argue that efficient firms mitigate these costs by aligning managerial incentives with performance goals, thereby minimizing resource waste. Additionally, they advocate for downsizing as a means to reduce organizational slack, lower overhead costs, and enhance operational efficiency, ultimately leading to improved financial performance (Geoffrey Love & Nohria, 2005; Williamson (2008)). 2.4 Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) suggests that firms reduce costs by minimizing inefficiencies in operations and governance. Efficient firms reduce production and coordination costs (e.g., via economies of scale or lean management), directly improving profitability. Studies using frontier analysis (e.g., SFA) show that firms with lower inefficiency scores achieve higher ROA and ROE (Greene & Segal, 2004). 2.5 Industrial Organization (IO) Theory IO theory links market structure to financial performance (Porter, 1981). Efficient firms exploit cost leadership strategies, undercutting rivals on price while maintaining margins. Empirical work shows that efficient firms (measured via DEA/SFA) outperform peers in competitive industries (Caves & Barton, 1990). 2.6 X-Efficiency Theory Leibenstein (1966) argues that firms often operate below maximum efficiency due to organizational slack. Eliminating such inefficiencies (e.g., via benchmarking with DEA) directly raises profitability. Research confirms that efficiency gains predict future earnings (Baik et al., 2013). 3. Literature Review The measurement of operational efficiency and its impact on performance varies significantly across methodological approaches. Nguyen et al. (2021) employed DEA to estimate three distinct efficiency measures - technical, pure technical, and scale efficiency - finding through panel regression analysis that these measures have differential effects on ROA and market-to-book ratios, with controlling shareholders significantly moderating these relationships. Similarly, (Baik et al., 2013) utilized both DEA and Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA), complemented by Malmquist index calculations, to demonstrate that changes in these efficiency measures positively predict future profitability beyond traditional financial ratios. 154 In the Nigerian manufacturing sector, Dahunsi and Soetan (2022) applied SFA with a Cobb-Douglas production function to derive technical efficiency scores, revealing through System-GMM estimation that these scores explained 29% of output variation and positively correlated with firm performance. Contrasting results emerged from financial market studies: Nguyen and Swanson (2009) used SFA efficiency measures to show inefficient firms surprisingly outperformed efficient ones in equity returns, while Chuan’Chewie’Ang et al. (2021) replicated this paradoxical finding in Australian markets using similar SFA-derived efficiency scores. Ting et al. (2024) implemented a novel approach by combining DEA efficiency scores with bootstrapped mediation analysis (5,000 samples) on Malaysian firms, demonstrating these efficiency measures partially mediate the ownership-performance relationship. The application of ML in predicting firm performance has evolved significantly, with studies demonstrating the superiority of these approaches over traditional statistical methods. Early work by Anand et al. (2019) established the effectiveness of random forests with classification trees, achieving 57-64% accuracy in predicting directional changes in five profitability measures (ROE, ROA, RNOA, CFO, FCF), particularly for cash flow-based metrics. Their findings revealed that accruals provided incremental predictive power beyond cash flows, with consistent accuracy across 1-5 year horizons. Building on this foundation, Vukovic et al. (2023) conducted a comprehensive comparison of methods for retail firms, testing random effects regression against various ML approaches including DNN, LSTM, and Random Forest, as well as ensemble methods. Their analysis of 551 firms demonstrated that previous profitability showed the strongest predictive power (β = 0.42, p<0.01), with sales growth and web traffic exhibiting nonlinear positive effects. Notably, advanced ensembles outperformed single algorithms, with LSTM networks proving particularly effective at capturing temporal patterns. Recent advances in neural network applications have pushed the boundaries of predictive performance. Montesinos (2022) implemented deep learning with 15 financial variables as inputs, comparing DNN against four baseline models for next-year profitability prediction. The DNN achieved an impressive F1-score of 0.81 (versus 0.68 for the best baseline), with feature importance analysis revealing current ROA (22% contribution), debt ratio (18%), and inventory turnover (15%) as key predictors. Similarly, Tutcu et al. (2024) focused on the IT sector with a three-hidden-layer ANN architecture (32-16-8 nodes), demonstrating superior performance (RMSE = 0.14) compared to MLR and decision trees, while also noting the increasing importance of market-specific factors post-2018. Zhou et al. (2022) introduced a new deep learning model, SNN-CNN, which combines self-organizing maps (SOM) and convolutional neural networks (CNN) for predicting financial performance. Using web-scraped financial data, the model classifies company performance into five levels. Findings revealed that high-performing enterprises have balanced financial indicators and stable development, while low-performing ones struggle with profitability and growth. Their proposed SNN-CNN model achieved a high prediction accuracy compared to traditional risk prediction models. Specialized applications have further expanded the scope of ML in performance prediction. Ylinen & Ranta (2024) employed XGBoost with SHAP/SAGE values to analyze corporate culture using 250,000 employee reviews, identifying overall culture (SAGE = 0.29), organizational pride (0.25), and job security (0.22) as top predictors of firm value and operating performance. D’Amato et al. (2024) incorporated ESG factors for EuroStoxx-600 firms, using partial dependence plots to reveal a nonlinear threshold effect at an ESG score of 65/100, with the strongest EBIT prediction occurring in the 70-85 range. SHAP values further demonstrated that environmental factors were most impactful among ESG components. Hybrid approaches combining traditional efficiency measures with ML have yielded particularly insightful results. Nandy and Singh (2020) developed an innovative two-stage framework that first applied DEA efficiency scoring to 450 paddy farms, followed by Random Forest analysis of efficiency determinants. Their results identified land ownership as the top predictor (Gini importance = 0.38), with education and credit access also playing significant roles, and demonstrated that the hybrid approach improved prediction R² by 22% compared to DEA alone. Expanding this methodology to manufacturing, Perroni et al. (2024) compared DEA versus SFA efficiency inputs across six ML algorithms applied to 7,548 US firms. Their analysis revealed that DEA-VRS with Random Forest achieved the best performance (AUC = 0.87), while SFA-LOG with SVM showed the strongest regression fit (R² = 0.63), highlighting the context-dependent nature of model effectiveness. These studies collectively demonstrate how the choice of efficiency measurement - whether DEA, SFA, or hybrid approaches - fundamentally shapes our understanding of the efficiency-performance relationship. The consistency of frontier methods (DEA/SFA) across studies allows for meaningful comparisons, while the growing incorporation of ML techniques points to new avenues for capturing complex, nonlinear relationships between efficiency and performance outcomes. The methodological evolution from early random forest applications to contemporary ensemble and deep learning architectures reveals several key trends. First, increasing model complexity has been matched by improved accuracy, though at the cost of greater computational requirements. Second, there has been growing emphasis on interpretability through techniques like SHAP and SAGE values. While ML has significantly enhanced the accuracy of financial performance prediction, several methodological gaps remain. Notably, few studies have explored the use of advanced ML to identify nonlinear or threshold effects in the relationship between efficiency and performance. A major limitation lies in the lack of explainability and interpretability; most ML models, such as deep learning and ensemble methods, function as “black boxes,” providing high predictive accuracy but limited insight into how input variables influence outcomes. Although tools like SHAP, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and counterfactual analysis offer potential for greater transparency, their adoption in the literature remains limited. DEA is a non-parametric method used to evaluate the relative efficiency of decision-making units (DMUs), such as firms or departments, by comparing their ability to convert multiple inputs into multiple outputs (Charnes et al., 1978). Unlike traditional financial ratios, DEA constructs a "best-practice frontier" based on observed data, where DMUs on the frontier are considered fully efficient (assigned a score of 1), while those below the frontier are deemed inefficient (scores < 1). This approach allows for a more nuanced assessment of performance by accounting for multiple operational factors simultaneously (Cooper et al., 2007). A key advantage of DEA is its ability to handle multiple inputs and outputs without requiring predefined weights. The study uses total assets (TA), cost of goods sold (COGS), and selling, general, and administrative expenses (SG&A) as inputs, with sales revenue as the sole output. This flexibility allows DEA to capture complex trade-offs—such as higher SG&A expenses potentially driving disproportionate sales growth—that simple financial ratios (e.g., asset turnover) cannot (Demerjian et al., 2012). By compensating for the limitations of individual algorithms and benefiting from their collective strengths, ensemble methods have been shown to outperform single models in predictive accuracy (Kunapuli, 2023; Mohammed & Kora, 2023; Thabet et al., 2024). Ensemble techniques are broadly classified into homogeneous and heterogeneous categories. Homogeneous ensembles use the same algorithm across different data subsets and include methods such as bagging and boosting. Bagging algorithms like RF and Extra Trees train models in parallel; RF is used as a base learner in this study. Boosting algorithms, which train models sequentially to correct prior errors, include AdaBoost, Gradient Boosted Regression Trees (GBR), LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost, with CatBoost also serving as a base learner in this research and others used for benchmarking. Heterogeneous ensembles, on the other hand, combine different types of ML models to improve predictive accuracy and generalization. This approach involves training diverse base learners on the same dataset, selecting the most effective models, and aggregating their outputs through either voting schemes or a meta-learning framework. Voting methods include majority, average, and weighted voting—the latter assigning importance based on each model’s performance. Meta-learning, by contrast, uses a second-level model (meta-learner) to determine the optimal way to combine the predictions of base learners, thereby constructing a stacked ensemble. These strategies are particularly effective in capturing complex patterns in both regression and classification tasks by leveraging model diversity and data-driven aggregation. The Super learner model is a stacking-based ensemble learning algorithm introduced by Van der Laan et al. (2007). The Super Learner is designed to overcome limitations of traditional ML approaches. By optimally combining multiple base models through a meta-learning framework, it achieves asymptotically optimal performance (Dey & Mathur, 2023; Naimi & Balzer, 2018; Phillips et al., 2023). Unlike single-model approaches, the Super Learner intelligently weights and integrates predictions from diverse algorithms, maximizing both accuracy and robustness. This makes it particularly valuable for complex prediction tasks where no single model consistently performs best. Research demonstrates the Super Learner's consistent outperformance of individual models across diverse datasets. This adaptability stems from its ability to dynamically select and weight the most effective base models for each specific prediction task. The method also reduces overfitting by excluding poorly performing models, thereby improving generalization on new data (Wong et al., 2019). The Super Learner's meta-learner plays a crucial role in its success. During training, this component 158 minimizes estimation errors by finding the optimal combination of base model predictions. Studies in behavior classification have shown this approach yields higher accuracy and lower variance compared to both individual models and traditional ensembles (Ladds et al., 2017). The meta-learning framework ensures the ensemble leverages each algorithm's strengths while mitigating weaknesses, leading to more reliable predictions. The Super Learner ensemble machine learning approach offers several advantages in predictive modeling and anomaly detection. It combines diverse base algorithms to create a powerful prediction function through metalearning, asymptotically performing at least as well as the best candidate (Davies & van der Laan, 2016; LeDell, 2015). This method has shown superior performance in spatial prediction problems and network security applications (Davies & van der Laan, 2016; Vanerio & Casas, 2017). Drawing from the Resource-Based View (RBV), the significant contribution of DEA efficiency scores to predictive performance supports the idea that operational efficiency constitutes a unique and valuable resource that firms can leverage to gain competitive advantage (Barney, 1991; Demerjian et al., 2012). The enhancement in model accuracy upon the inclusion of the DEA variable—an R² increase of 3.8% with a statistically significant t-statistic of 5.45—corroborates empirical studies that emphasize the predictive power of frontier efficiency measures (Baik et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2021). Moreover, the results validate principles of Dynamic Capabilities Theory by illustrating how high-efficiency firms outperform others, particularly at DEA levels exceeding 0.8. The nonlinear pattern revealed in the partial dependence plots supports the concept that firms continuously improving their operational configurations—through just-in-time systems or technology adoption—achieve sustainable performance gains (Färe et al., 1992; Teece et al., 1997). These nonlinearities, undetectable in traditional linear models, are made visible through ML techniques, reinforcing recent methodological innovations in performance prediction (Montesinos, 2022; Perroni et al., 2024). The observed threshold effects also echo findings from Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) and Agency Theory. This reflects Williamson’s (2008) view that efficient governance minimizes costs, and Jensen & Meckling (1976) argument that reducing agency slack through efficient operations leads to improved outcomes. The SHAP analysis further reinforces this view, showing that DEA and liquidity-related variables (NETCAP and CASH) positively influence financial performance. In line with X-Efficiency Theory (Leibenstein, 1966), the study shows that firms operating below optimal efficiency—indicated by DEA scores under 0.6—fail to realize substantial performance gains, whereas those nearing full efficiency benefit disproportionately. This trend is similarly evident in variables like NETCAP and CASH, where gains taper off after certain thresholds, consistent with the findings of Ting et al. (2024). Additionally, the results confirm the advantages of hybrid methodologies. The superior performance of the Super Learner 166 model (R² = 0.612) relative to both individual models and traditional ensembles supports the literature’s emphasis on model integration to capture complex efficiency-performance dynamics (Anand et al., 2019; Vukovic et al., 2023). The model’s ability to outperform linear and nonlinear baselines highlights the relevance of ML frameworks in complementing frontier efficiency methods (Nandy & Singh, 2020; Perroni et al., 2024). Importantly, the inclusion of interpretable ML techniques such as SHAP adds further value. These tools illuminate how specific variables affect model predictions, addressing longstanding criticisms regarding the opacity of ML (Ylinen & Ranta, 2024). For instance, the identification of NETCAP as the strongest predictor of financial performance, along with the nuanced impact of dividends and leverage, provides practical implications for financial management and strategic planning. In sum, this study’s findings substantiate the theoretical claims that operational efficiency—measured via DEA—significantly contributes to financial performance. The integration of advanced ML techniques, particularly the Super Learner ensemble, not only enhances predictive accuracy but also enables deeper insights into the mechanisms through which efficiency and financial indicators influence outcomes. These insights are especially critical in emerging markets, such as Egypt, where firm characteristics and regulatory contexts may differ significantly from those in more developed economies. Thus, this research bridges the gap between theoretical expectations and empirical application, offering a robust and interpretable framework for understanding and predicting financial performance. 6 Conclusion This study provides compelling evidence that incorporating operational efficiency—measured through DEA—significantly enhances the predictive accuracy of financial performance models. By leveraging a Super Learner ensemble framework, which integrates RF and CatBoost algorithms with a linear regression meta-learner, the research demonstrates that efficiency is not only a statistically significant predictor but also one of the most influential factors shaping firm outcomes. The improvement in predictive performance, as indicated by the increase in R² from 0.574 to 0.612, underscores the added value of DEA in capturing dimensions of operational effectiveness that are often overlooked by traditional financial metrics. The findings carry important implications for various stakeholders. For corporate managers, the results highlight the critical role of operational efficiency, working capital management, and prudent capital structure in driving financial performance. This suggests that beyond financial reporting, attention to internal resource utilization can yield substantial strategic benefits. Investors and financial analysts can use efficiency scores as complementary indicators when assessing firm quality and future profitability, particularly in emerging markets where conventional financial signals may be noisy or distorted. Policymakers and regulators, especially in developing economies like Egypt, may also find value in promoting transparency and benchmarking practices that encourage firms to enhance their efficiency, ultimately contributing to broader economic development and competitiveness. Despite its contributions, the study is not without limitations. First, the sample is limited to non-financial firms listed on the Egyptian Stock Exchange, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to other contexts or industries. Second, while DEA provides a robust framework for measuring efficiency, it does not account for random noise or measurement errors, which stochastic frontier models might better capture. Third, although the Super Learner ensemble improves prediction, it adds model complexity and requires higher computational resources. Future research can address these limitations by extending the analysis to different sectors, countries, or time periods to enhance external validity. Incorporating alternative efficiency measures, such as Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) or hybrid DEA-SFA models, may offer a more nuanced understanding of financial performance dynamics. In conclusion, this study bridges a critical gap between theoretical insights and practical application by demonstrating that operational efficiency is not only conceptually important but also empirically potent in predicting financial performance. By combining frontier efficiency analysis with cutting-edge ML, it provides a scalable and interpretable framework for performance forecasting, offering tangible benefits for both academic inquiry and real-world decision-making. JSON: Name: dea_superlearner_roa Title: An explainable Super Learner ensemble integrating DEA-based frontier efficiency for predicting firm financial performance (ROA) Short Hypothesis: Including DEA-derived operational efficiency as an input feature in a Super Learner ensemble (RF + CatBoost base learners, linear meta-learner) causes a statistically significant increase in out-of-sample R2 for next-year ROA predictions compared to the identical ensemble trained without the DEA feature. Related Work: Existing approaches to firm performance prediction fall into three main families: (1) ratio-based linear regression models that use financial ratios (widely used but limited by linearity assumptions and susceptibility to accounting manipulation); (2) frontier efficiency methods (DEA, SFA) that measure relative operational efficiency and have been used to explain performance but are rarely integrated directly into predictive ML pipelines and do not model noise (DEA) or require functional-form assumptions (SFA); (3) machine learning methods (tree ensembles, boosting, neural networks, LSTM) and ensemble strategies that capture nonlinearities and temporal patterns but often act as black boxes and are sensitive to hyperparameters and sample size. Hybrid studies that combine DEA with ML are limited and typically use DEA as a secondary target or explanatory stage rather than as a predictive feature; ensemble fusion methods (voting, simple stacking) have shown gains but may use fixed aggregation rules and lack adaptive meta-learning. Gaps include limited evaluation of DEA as an explicit predictor in advanced stacking/Super Learner frameworks, scarce ablation analyses isolating efficiency contributions, and insufficient use of explainability tools to relate frontier scores to ML predictions. Abstract: Predicting firm financial performance reliably is essential for investors, lenders, and managers, yet traditional ratio-based models and standalone machine learning methods either miss nonlinear patterns or lack interpretability. This research proposes an interpretable predictive pipeline that integrates Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) frontier efficiency scores as explicit features into a Super Learner stacking ensemble (Random Forest and CatBoost base learners with a linear meta-learner) to forecast next-year Return on Assets (ROA). The contribution is a reproducible, explainable hybrid workflow that quantifies the marginal predictive value of operational efficiency and uses model-agnostic explanations to reveal nonlinear effects and thresholds. Expected outcomes are (1) improved out-of-sample predictive accuracy versus baseline linear and single-model ML approaches, (2) a quantified contribution of DEA to predictive performance, and (3) transparent mappings from inputs to ROA predictions that identify nonlinear and concave relationships for key financial controls. The pipeline is designed for adoption on medium-scale firm-year datasets in emerging markets and aims to produce actionable, testable insights for stakeholders. Experiments: Datasets: non-financial firms listed on the Egyptian Stock Exchange, 2016–2022; sample selection: exclude financial-sector firms and foreign-currency reporters; expected sample: 104 firms, ~699 firm-year observations after preprocessing. Feature set: ROA (next-year) target; predictors include 12 financial and firm controls plus DEA efficiency scores (DEA inputs: total assets, COGS, SG&A; output: sales revenue). Preprocessing: median imputation for missing values; winsorization at 5th–95th percentiles; standardization where required. Baselines: (A) linear models: OLS, Ridge, Lasso; (B) single ML: Random Forest, CatBoost, XGBoost, SVR, MLP; (C) ensemble variants: voting ensemble, standard stacked ensemble; (D) Super Learner with DEA and Super Learner excluding DEA (ablation). Additional ablations: meta-learner variants (linear vs ridge), single-base ablations (RF-only, CatBoost-only), and hyperparameter tuning ablation (random-search tuned vs default). Evaluation metrics: out-of-sample R2, RMSE, MAE; complemented by paired statistical test on R2 differences (e.g., paired t-test or Diebold-Mariano on squared errors) and calibration plots. Experimental setup: random seed fixed; stratified 80/20 train/test split by firm-year with blocked CV to avoid temporal leakage; 10-fold cross-validation on training set for hyperparameter tuning using random search (predefined parameter ranges) and nested validation for stacking; report mean and 95% CI over 20 repeated splits. Explainability: compute global feature importances (CatBoost) and SHAP values plus partial dependence plots for top predictors. Success criteria: Super Learner with DEA yields higher mean test R2 than Super Learner without DEA with p<0.01 and lower RMSE and MAE. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data representativeness: sample restricted to Egyptian non-financial listed firms limits external validity to other countries, private firms, or financial sector. DEA measurement: DEA scores are deterministic and sensitive to input/output selection and outliers; they do not separate inefficiency from statistical noise. Sample size and sparsity: moderate sample (~700 observations) may constrain complex model generalization and amplify hyperparameter overfitting risk. Temporal leakage and nonstationarity: macroeconomic shocks or regime changes during 2016–2022 can alter relationships, reducing temporal transferability. Model complexity and compute: Super Learner stacking with tuned tree ensembles increases compute and memory requirements and may impede real-time deployment. Interpretability limits: SHAP and PDP explain associations, not causal effects; multicollinearity between financial predictors and DEA may confound attributions. Evaluation bias: chosen train/test splits and preprocessing choices (winsorization, imputation) can bias performance estimates. Statistical testing: comparing R2 across models requires careful paired testing and may be sensitive to heteroskedasticity. Finally, policy or managerial actions based on model outputs risk misinterpretation if users conflate predictive associations with causal relationships.
